Threat.value: I feel on guard even inside my own home
Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame
Being superalert or watchful or on guard

Memory.value: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened.
When I remember the frightening event I feel like it is happening right now.
My memories of the event feel more real and vivid than memories of ordinary things

Negative Appraisals.value: I have lost my faith in people, life, or a higher power
The world is a dangerous place
My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe

issues.item: Humiliation: I feel permanently humiliated by what happened
issues.explanation: For a life-threatening illness trauma, 'permanently humiliated' is hard to reconcile unless the illness involved a specifically shaming interpersonal circumstance; nothing else in the profile suggests that context. The other items center danger, fear, vivid reliving, and generalized threat, so humiliation stands out as clinically mismatched to the trauma type.

vignette: Emmett's world shrunk to the size of his hospital room on the day he received his cancer diagnosis. The antiseptic smell that clung to every surface has lingered in his memory ever since, wafting up unexpectedly when he least expects it - a pungent reminder of the fear that gripped him as he listened to the doctor's words. Even now, two years later, Emmett can recall the sensation of the bed beneath him, the beeping of machines, and the feeling of his life slipping out from under his control. As he navigates his daily routine, these sensory memories intrude upon his thoughts, making it feel as though the past is more real than the present. When he remembers that day, Emmett feels like he's reliving it - his heart racing, his breath catching in his throat. It's a sensation that has left him with a lingering sense of unease, a feeling that his body is still reacting to the danger even though he's safe now. This discord between his mind and body has led Emmett to believe that his own flesh is an unreliable ally, prone to betraying him at any moment. The memories have also taken a toll on Emmett's worldview. He used to find solace in his faith, but after his diagnosis, he began to question whether there was anyone - or anything - looking out for him. The world now seems like a capricious and unforgiving place, where tragedy can strike without warning. His lost faith has left him feeling disconnected from the people around him, even those who care about him deeply. Emmett's hypervigilance is another legacy of that hospital stay. He feels on guard even in his own home, constantly scanning for potential threats - a creaking floorboard, an unfamiliar noise outside. This alertness has become exhausting, making it difficult for him to relax or let his defenses down. When he does manage to calm himself, Emmett is often struck by the realization that his body remains tense, as though still bracing itself for some unseen blow. As a database administrator, Emmett's job requires attention to detail and analytical thinking - skills that have become increasingly difficult for him to access in recent months. His inability to focus has led to mistakes at work, which only serves to reinforce his growing sense of unease about the world around him. The danger he perceives is no longer just medical; it's also professional, threatening to upend the fragile stability he's managed to establish. For Emmett, seeking help now feels like a last resort - an admission that he can't manage on his own anymore. He hopes that therapy will provide some respite from the relentless cycle of threat and memory, allowing him to rebuild his faith in himself, others, and the world around him. What he fears most is being trapped forever in this state of hyperarousal, unable to escape the lingering shadows of his illness.
